title: Linux Matters homepage: fixed nav, banner, subscribe badges, episode grid
stressor: a real-world Bootstrap-grid podcast homepage with a fixed nav, banner, subscribe-badge row, multi-column episode card grid, and pagination - real page structure that scrolls, used to catch overlay scroll-dance regressions across snapshot generations
attribution: Markup and copy frozen from the live Linux Matters homepage on 2026-07-04 for offline corpus use. Provenance only: Linux Matters is the maintainer's own project.
notes: Self-contained single page, all CSS inline, no script, no network URLs. Frozen from https://linuxmatters.sh/ on 2026-07-04. Bootstrap 4.6.2, Font Awesome, mediaelement, and Google Fonts Poppins are not loaded; the kept Bootstrap grid classes are re-styled with plain inline CSS at the md breakpoint for a 960px viewport, and Poppins falls back to a generic sans-serif. Structure: a fixed-top nav bar, an episode banner with a number overlay, a Show Summary block, a jumbotron with intro copy plus three round host avatars and a subscribe-badge row, a three-column Past Episodes card grid, a pagination row, and a footer. All images are placeholder solid-fill data URIs at the real display dimensions; geometry matters, pixels do not. Designed to be tall enough to scroll for the scroll-dance leg. Placement gates cleanly on the current build at all three geometries: 120x40 mean 0.240 max 0.500; 240x48 and the real-geometry 158x86 leg (cell 16x33, layout_scale 1.975) mean about 0.26 max 0.500; drifted 0, collisions 0, offgrid 0 everywhere. The scroll-dance leg is a hard gate at danced 0. The scroll-dance metric classifies the position:fixed nav (13 runs that stay at the viewport top on scroll) as fixed and scores every other run on its own scroll-compensated document row round((Y+scrollY)/cellH), so a fixed nav and scrolling body content each read honestly rather than the fixed nav counting against the body's median shift. The compose-time scroll shift re-snaps each run's cell from the shifted box origin the same way mapBoxToCells decodes, so a mid-scroll frame and the settle re-decode land the same row and no body run hops one cell when the scroll settles. Together these score danced 0 and re-placements 0 on both legs at 158x86 cell 16x33 capture=3 scroll=600; scroll_dance_gate carries the matched-run counts. The shift also reads the anchor flag and the viewport-anchored boxes the walk reports beside the runs, so it holds a run that descends from the fixed nav in place instead of translating it, and drops a body run that the shift moves under the nav's opaque background. That is what makes the mid-scroll frame agree with the settled one on this page: before it, the pre-settle frame classified 0 runs as fixed, because the shift had slid the nav's own text off the nav.

scroll_dance_gate.reason: Hard-gate thresholds, met on the current build: danced 0 and re-placements 0 on both legs at 158x86 cell 16x33 capture=3 scroll=600. The metric classifies the position:fixed nav as viewport-stationary rather than counting it against the body's scroll, and the compose shift re-snaps from the shifted box origin so no body run hops a row at settle. Keep danced 0 and replacements 0 as the regression guard. The approved run counts alongside this gate were re-measured when the shift learned to hold viewport-anchored runs: the mid-scroll leg reads 56 matched runs, 13 fixed nav and 43 glued body, against 46 matched, 0 fixed and 46 body before that change, so the change costs 3 body runs mid-scroll and buys the 13-run fixed cohort; the settled leg is unchanged at 61 matched, 13 fixed nav and 48 glued body. Those are the numbers cdpScrollApprovedPreRuns, cdpScrollApprovedPreBody, cdpScrollApprovedSettleBody and cdpScrollApprovedFixedRuns hold, exactly, with cdpScrollRunTolerance supplying the whole slack. Both legs held them across eight consecutive runs on this branch and one on the pre-change baseline. Commit 35ad06a's message misreports that baseline as 47 matched runs and 47 body, and so counts 4 culled body runs where measurement gives 3; the message is in published history and stays wrong, so trust these figures over it.
